title: How Wealth Inequality Emerged in This Prehistoric Culture - Nautilus
gist: A Journal of Neolithic Archaeology study using the QuantWealth framework on ~300 Corded Ware graves in Bohemia finds inequality emerged gradually in three phases — cooperation, funerary competition, then inherited wealth tied to a dominant Y-chromosome lineage — rather than being imported wholesale by steppe migrants.

insights.claim: A Journal of Neolithic Archaeology study examined how the contents and genetics of nearly 300 Corded Ware graves in ancient Bohemia (roughly 2900–2300 BCE) changed over time to trace the emergence of wealth inequality.
insights.so_what: Deep-history evidence on how inequality forms.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: The QuantWealth framework scores grave goods by manufacturing time, scarcity, distance of origin and the weight of meat offerings to quantify the deceased's affluence.
insights.so_what: A replicable method for quantifying wealth in archaeological data.
insights.locator: According to the team, the objects
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Mikkel Nørtoft of the University of Copenhagen says the results contradict the idea that steppe migrants from Ukraine imported a highly unequal, patriarchal system, pointing instead to social differences that developed gradually.
insights.so_what: Challenges diffusion-based explanations of social stratification.
insights.quote: Our results suggest a much more dynamic picture, where social differences developed gradually.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: The earliest Corded Ware phase in Bohemia, beginning after a volcanic event cooled global temperatures, was cooperative, with muted wealth display, shared burial rituals and earthen mounds but few grave goods.
insights.so_what: Suggests climate shocks can foster social cohesion over competition.
insights.quote: In Bohemia, they did this through shared burial rituals, and building earthen mounds, but with few grave goods
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Between 2,700 and 2,500 BCE, funerary competition rose with more prestige items and meat offerings, adult male graves grew more ornate, and a new Y-chromosome haplogroup appeared, which the researchers read as possible patrilineal power struggles.
insights.so_what: Links genetic lineage dominance to rising gender and wealth inequality.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: In the final phase, the new Y-chromosome lineage dominated and a few richly decorated child graves with copper rings suggest inherited wealth and the start of persistent inequality.
insights.so_what: Inheritance, not individual achievement, marks the onset of durable inequality.
insights.quote: The few rich child graves and this prevailing lineage could indicate more inherited wealth and emerging traits of persistent inequality
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
